alt: Seven stages of research design in order: selection of topic, aims, hypothesis, target population, methods, operationalisation and pilot study, each with an example from the lesson. Operationalisation is highlighted: social class might be measured by parents’ occupation.
caption: Research is a chain of decisions, and each stage limits the next.

alt: Structured, semi-structured and unstructured interviews placed on a line from more comparable and reliable to more depth and validity, with group interviews below. Ann Oakley’s 1974 in-depth interviews with 40 London housewives are the example.
caption: The less structured the interview, the more depth it gives and the harder it is to compare.

alt: A grid of observation types. Overt participant: Whyte’s Street Corner Society (1943) gained access through “Doc”, allowing consent but risking the observer effect. Covert participant: Patrick secretly joined a Glasgow gang (1973), reducing the observer effect but using deception. Non-participant: watching a classroom from the back.
caption: Participant or not, overt or covert: two separate choices.

alt: A table of four question types with an example and use: open questions give answers in the respondent’s own words, closed questions give quick yes or no answers, multiple choice offers several countable options, and scaled questions measure strength of opinion.
caption: Open questions favour validity; closed and scaled questions favour comparison.

alt: Three groups of pressure on method choice. Theoretical: positivists favour questionnaires and structured interviews, interpretivists unstructured interviews and participant observation. Practical: access, response rate, funding and time. Ethical: informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, deception, prevention of harm and legality.
caption: Every method choice balances theory, practicality and ethics.

alt: Left: the steps of Laud Humphreys’s Tearoom Trade (1970), from covert observation to noting car numbers, tracing addresses and interviewing men in disguise. Right: the five ethical issues it raised: no informed consent, risk to privacy, deception, potential harm and questions of legality.
caption: Tearoom Trade breached all five ethical principles the syllabus names.

after: ## Worked example: a research plan for part (e)
alt: A research plan on how teenagers choose subjects, set out as choice and reason: semi-structured interviews for depth and comparison, a pilot to check questions, a stratified sample from three schools’ registers, national subject-entry figures for context, and informed consent with confidentiality.
caption: Name each choice and justify it against the aim; do not evaluate.
